note: Teaching text, clarifying questions, inferred constraints and own examples. Inferred, not official. Examples are small generated inputs with outputs from the independent references in oracles.py.

constraints: ids passed to methods always exist
clarifyingQuestions: Does referral credit propagate beyond the direct referrer?
What happens with an unknown referrer id?
Are credits fractional?
hints: An account total only changes when it is created or when it refers someone.
Keep one running total per id.
On a referral, add the new credit to both the new slot and the referrer slot.
invariants: totals[i] = own credit of i + credits of accounts directly referred by i
next id = number of accounts
chooseWhen: Totals are queried often and accounts are only added
tradeoffs: O(1) updates; storing referral edges is unnecessary for level 1
hack2hire:6aa32d070ca9cc4e1c790398.variantLabel: Inferred level 1: account totals with direct referral credit

constraints: ids passed to methods always exist
clarifyingQuestions: Does referral credit propagate beyond the direct referrer?
What happens with an unknown referrer id?
Are credits fractional?
How are ties in the ranking broken?
hints: Totals only grow, but several accounts can change between queries.
A heap keyed by (-total, id) gives the ranking; old entries go stale when a total changes.
Skip entries whose stored total differs from the current total, and push the k winners back after the query.
invariants: every account has at least one heap entry holding its current total
stale entries are never returned
chooseWhen: Many updates interleaved with small-k ranking queries
tradeoffs: Lazy deletion grows the heap by one entry per update; a balanced tree would avoid stale entries
hack2hire:6aa32de80ca9cc4e1c7903a3.variantLabel: Inferred level 2: top accounts by total credit

constraints: up to 3000 commands of at most 100 printable ASCII characters
clarifyingQuestions: Which distance metric is used for routing?
How are ties between equally near datacenters broken?
What does ROUTE return when no datacenter qualifies?
hints: Validate the whole command before changing any state.
Squared distance stays an exact integer, so no square root is needed.
Scan eligible datacenters once, keeping the best (distance, load, name) triple.
invariants: a failed command leaves the router unchanged
load never exceeds capacity
chooseWhen: Few datacenters and a text command protocol
tradeoffs: A linear scan per ROUTE is simple; a spatial index would pay off only for many datacenters

constraints: snapshot ids in queries refer to taken snapshots
clarifyingQuestions: What does snapshot() return?
Is unfollowing a missing edge an error?
Can a query name a snapshot that has not been taken?
hints: Copying the whole graph at every snapshot is too expensive.
Record each edge change against the current snapshot counter (Snapshot Array idea).
Answer a query by binary-searching that edge history for the last change at or before the snapshot.
invariants: per-edge history snapshot ids are strictly increasing
the last entry for the current counter reflects the working state
chooseWhen: Many snapshots with few changes between them
tradeoffs: History per edge costs O(changes); queries pay O(log h)

constraints: snapshot ids in queries refer to taken snapshots
clarifyingQuestions: What does snapshot() return?

hints: A user's followees at a snapshot are a subset of every followee they ever touched.

constraints: snapshot ids in queries refer to taken snapshots
clarifyingQuestions: What does snapshot() return?
Is unfollowing a missing edge an error?
Can a query name a snapshot that has not been taken?
How are recommendations scored and ordered?
hints: Recommendations come from two hops in the snapshot graph.
Count, for each second-hop user, how many direct followees lead to it.
Exclude the user and anyone already followed, then sort by (-score, id).
invariants: scores count distinct followees
excluded users never appear
chooseWhen: Small fan-out graphs queried at past snapshots
tradeoffs: Two-hop expansion is O(d^2) per query

constraints: up to 300 listings, at most 60000 listed days in total
clarifyingQuestions: Can a split use more than two listings?
Is [i, j] different from [j, i]?
Should pairs be listed when one listing alone suffices?
hints: Each listing only matters through how far it extends from start and how far back it reaches from end.
Walk forward from start while the day is available; walk back from end likewise.
A pair (i, j) works iff j's suffix starts no later than one day after i's prefix ends, with both parts non-empty.
invariants: prefixEnd[i] >= start iff i covers start
suffixStart[j] <= end iff j covers end
tradeoffs: Output can be quadratic in the number of listings
hack2hire:68baf390b5314dcd938cba02.variantLabel: Inferred: single and two-listing split stays

clarifyingQuestions: Are duplicates in a removed or kept?
What should next() do when exhausted?
Can the iterator copy the arrays?
hints: Membership in b is the only question asked about each a-element.
Put b's values in a hash set once.
Keep a cursor into b and one into a; hasNext advances the a-cursor past excluded values.
invariants: the a-cursor never rests on a value present in b after hasNext()
no input array is modified
tradeoffs: O(|b|) extra memory for the set

clarifyingQuestions: Is the answer a count, a minimum, or a yes/no?
Does the empty sequence count when initial == target?
Is a modulus required?
hints: Track how many sequences reach each holding after each step.
Sum the ways at target over every length 0..m.
Holdings above target + remaining steps can never come back, so cap the array.
invariants: ways[h] counts sequences of the current length ending at h without going negative
chooseWhen: Small m with exact modular counting
tradeoffs: O(m^2) DP; the closed form needs big binomials

Count distinct senders per receiver with a hash map.

clarifyingQuestions: When is the alert condition evaluated?
Is the window inclusive of both ends?
Can the same merchant and code alert more than once?
hints: Sort records by time and group by merchant.
Slide a window per merchant, keeping per-code sums.
A count only rises when that code has records at t, so check those codes there.
invariants: window sums equal the records inside [t-W+1, t]
each (merchant, code) alerts at most once
tradeoffs: Sorting dominates; per-code sums are O(codes) memory

clarifyingQuestions: When is the alert condition evaluated?
Is the window inclusive of both ends?
Can the same merchant and code alert more than once?
Is the rate relative to all transactions?
hints: The rate needs a running total next to per-code sums.
Compare errorCount*100 with percent*total to stay in integers.
The rate can cross the threshold when 200s leave the window, so check every code present.
invariants: total equals the sum of all per-code sums in the window
chooseWhen: Merchants with very different traffic volumes
tradeoffs: Checking all codes per evaluation is O(codes)

clarifyingQuestions: When is the alert condition evaluated?
Is the window inclusive of both ends?
Can the same merchant and code alert more than once?
When does an active alert resolve?
hints: Keep a set of active (merchant, code) alerts.
At each evaluation, an active code whose condition fails becomes inactive.
Include active codes that left the window: their count is zero, so they resolve.
invariants: an alert is emitted only on an inactive-to-active transition
tradeoffs: State per active alert; evaluation cost grows with active codes

constraints: 1 <= K <= 500 groups, at most 2000 distinct nodes
clarifyingQuestions: Must every valid answer be equally likely?
Is any valid answer accepted?
How is randomness supplied?
hints: Contract each group to a vertex; a tree on K vertices has a Pruefer sequence of length K-2.
Choosing a node (not a group) at each Pruefer position weights each group by its size; one extra node per group fixes the leaf-side endpoints.
Decode digits with big integers, then decode the Pruefer sequence with a min-heap of leaves.
invariants: every emitted edge joins two different groups
the decoded edges form a tree on the contracted groups
chooseWhen: Uniform random structures needing exact counting
tradeoffs: Big-integer ranks; a random generator would sample without them
hack2hire:6aa882a68c97c56cdbdc954f.variantLabel: Inferred: rank-indexed uniform spanning edge set

clarifyingQuestions: Should the schedules be returned or only counted?
In what order?
Can a fixed digit exceed dayHours?
hints: Subtract the fixed digits from workHours first.
Fill the ? positions left to right with increasing digits; the output is then sorted.
Prune when the remaining hours exceed what the remaining ? slots can hold.
invariants: partial sums never exceed workHours
chooseWhen: Outputs are small enough to list
tradeoffs: Pruning keeps work near the output size

clarifyingQuestions: What should be returned: the finish order or the last person?
Are indices 1-based?
hints: Simulation can take sum(amounts)/k turns, which is too many.
Person i finishes in round ceil(amounts[i]/k).
Within one round, people keep their original relative order.
invariants: queue order inside each round equals original order
tradeoffs: Sorting avoids a potentially huge simulation
